Exactly. I've been world building a cyber punk place for almost 20 years on and off. Some of it is on paper, but the majority of it is in my head. I''d explore our world quite a lot and take things I liked and exaggerated them. Then the world itself is just a cluttered mess as it is because everything is just built on top of eachother in a Modular fashion. The newer modular buildings are built upon a skeletal infrastructure made of lost tech metal materials strewn about the continent that would outline cities and make them earthquake proof. I also explore the presence and demeanor of my characters rather than just tell them what they would do. There's around like 9 central characters some which never meet, but sometimes have direct influence over eachothere etc. Most, like 97% is the world just naturally coming together.

That book of town names he has. I have something similar with Names of peoples and characters and just by the name alone I can vaguely remember their presence and write for them again.

All of my music I have on youtube is about this world as well from different characters.

I've been exploring this place for a very long time.

replies.author: @SmaskysButler
replies.text: How many rules could be followed before creativity is eliminated?

replies.author: @traaashking
replies.text:
​@SmaskysButler I've been doing creative work professionally for almost 10 years, and let me assure you that constraints, far from eliminating creativity, actually boost it.

In fact, creativity is a skill you have to develop and nurture through disciplined rules; without them, it loses focus and becomes impossible to sustain with any consistency.

Only the most superficial of amateur hobbyists who dabble intermittently without any commitment can afford no restrictions.

This is true for any creative endeavor, be it knitting, painting, programming, gardening, drumming, baking... whatever!

Does this mean you need to slavishly follow directives and never deviate from prescriptive norms? Of course not! But if you want to achieve specific results every time you attempt creative work, you need rules: A sponge cake needs a specific amount of heat for a certain amount of time or it'll deflate, code needs to be written with precision and good logic or it'll fail to compile and end up full of bugs, you need to study anatomy and color theory if you want to paint anything other than random blotches of abstraction on a canvas, you will never be able to improvise with fellow musicians unless you train yourself to keep time until it becomes intuition, you have to plant tomato seeds a couple of months before the summer if you want the best harvest, and your sweaters will unravel or fit wrong if you don't knit your yarn using the right stitches!

Limitations foster creativity!

replies.author: @ShadowOfCicero
replies.text: ​@SmaskysButlerOrson Scott Card, most famous for Ender's Game, once took a poetry class in college. After one too many free verse submissions, his professor told him, "Go write me a hundred sonnets." Card considered that project one of the key catalysts for his writing career. On some level, you have to know the rules to know how to break them.

The whole "the rules are in charge and I try to think as little as possible to get things to be as random as possible" shtick is really inspiring. A big reason I got into making videogames was making worlds that have some autonomy on their own so that even as a creator you get to explore the unknown, but I feel I've lost my way there (not fiddling as much with procgen after roguelikes got so oversaturated as a genre, and thinking too much about levels as disposable "content" instead of as a world).
I'm also reminded about that quote from Shigeru Miyamoto that you get the best ideas along the way, and if something turns out exactly as initially planned it's a failure.

topComment.author: @themediater
topComment.text: I'm reading a book called "Up in the Old Hotel" that's a collection of interviews and articles with folks who live in New York from all sorts of walks of life, written by a journalist over his career and Jerry feels like he would fit in with a lot of them, seems like a lovely, interesting bloke. Really makes me wish UBI was a thing, imagine how many people have some really wild stuff like this in them but will never even start down the road because they have to grind their lives into powder earning rent and barely enough even for that.

topComment.author: @scbtripwire
topComment.text: 37:38 This made me cry. Given his age it's possible this is the last time he will see it fully lain out. Mortality versus a lifetime of work brought into focus in one view.

replies.author: @PyroOfZen
replies.text: You will do everything you do for the last time, eventually. It's natural. Nothing will stop it. It's part of the process. Let it be, and accept that it is. Don't despair that it may be the last time he sees the map lain out. Rejoice that he got another opportunity. Anything could've happened in those 14 years to make the previous last time the definitive last time. Don't dwell on lasts denoting an ending. See them as "one more."
